transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-09 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~54m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Verdant Orbit), Rajan Patel (Verdant Security), Tom Wu (Platform)

Auto-generated summary (may be partial): Verdant Orbit is evaluating Redwood Private for a cross-region deployment that must stay on private network fabric across US-East and EU-West. Main concerns: transit gateway peering vs direct VPC peering, private endpoint types, egress controls and regional data residency, KMS/HSM integration, and audit logging. Next steps agreed: share peering examples, private endpoint options, SOC2/HSM docs, and schedule a deep-dive with Verdant networking.

Topics: private onramp, transit vs peering, private endpoints, region gating, encryption/KMS, SOC2/compliance, latency/cost tradeoffs

00:00:03 Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time today, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account; we've got Diego from our SE team. Can you each do a 30 second intros?
00:00:12 Lena Park: Yeah sure I'm Lena, lead cloud architect at Verdant Orbit, we run a hybrid infra - core in us-east-1 and some edge in eu-west-1 for european customers. We're looking at private deployment options.
00:00:23 Rajan Patel: Rajan, security lead, focused on data residency, KMS integration, and audit trails.
00:00:27 Tom Wu: Tom, platform, I own the onramp automation and transit gateway stuff.
00:00:33 Diego Ramos: Diego from Redwood; I look after private deployments and networking work with customers on peering, private endpoints, and on-prem connect.
00:00:42 Maya Chen: Cool, high level — are you evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private or is private the primary path?
00:00:47 Lena Park: Private is our primary path. We need the service inside our VPCs due to compliance and to avoid egress to public internet.
00:00:55 Maya Chen: Understood. Can you describe the topology you have today?
00:01:01 Tom Wu: Sure. Primary VPC in us-east-1 with TGW attached to multiple accounts. EU region has a smaller VPC with its own TGW, and we use inter-region peering via the cloud provider or a transit fabric. We also have some on-prem colo connecting via site-to-site.
00:01:17 Diego Ramos: Quick clarification — when you say TGW do you mean transit gateway or a third-party fabric?
00:01:21 Tom Wu: Transit gateway, sorry.
00:01:24 Diego Ramos: Cool. So typical options are: 1) Redwood Private deployed into your VPCs using private endpoints (PrivLink/PrivateLink or private endpoints depending on provider), 2) deploy in a dedicated VPC and peer it into your TGW, or 3) use a Transit Gateway attachment pattern with VPC attachments from Redwood-managed VPCs. Each has tradeoffs on routing complexity, IP footprint, and who manages the route tables.
00:01:43 Rajan Patel: For us key constraints: no public egress of PII, keys must be customer-managed KMS/HSM, audit logs need to land in our Splunk and be unredacted for regulatory review. We also need SSO (SAML) and per-team RBAC.
00:02:03 Diego Ramos: All of those are supported. Redwood Private can integrate with customer KMS via external key wrapping — we have a few patterns: KMS cross-account grants, or HSM-backed wrapping for air-gapped installs. Our audit logs can stream to customer endpoints via syslog/S3 hooks and we can push structured traces to your Splunk using our log-forwarder.
00:02:19 Rajan Patel: How about latency for cross-region calls? If we keep some models in us-east and others in eu-west, what's the recommended approach?
00:02:28 Diego Ramos: If you need sub-100ms tail latency, you generally want model instances co-located with the region traffic. For cross-region inference we typically route by policy — low-latency routes go to local region, fallback to another region for capacity/DR. There's a cost tradeoff: duplicating models per region increases cost but keeps latency predictable.
00:02:45 Maya Chen: Are you planning to pin model versions or use Redwood model catalog?
00:02:49 Lena Park: We'll likely pin specific verified open models for production, but might use catalog variants for testing.
00:02:54 Diego Ramos: Okay. On network side, two big decisions: do you want Redwood's control plane in our hosted control plane with data plane in your VPCs, or fully private control plane inside your network? Fully private control plane is possible but increases onboarding time and requires dedicated networking.
00:03:10 Tom Wu: We prefer control plane in our environment if possible due to policy.
00:03:14 Diego Ramos: Noted. We can run a private control plane behind your SAML SSO and connect the data plane nodes via private endpoints. That setup has been done for several regulated customers; it requires mutual TLS and customer-managed certs.
00:03:28 Lena Park: On peering: we run a /16 in us-east and /18 in eu-west; our concern is overlapping CIDRs if Redwood deploys into a separate VPC. Do you prefer TGW attachment or direct peering?
00:03:40 Diego Ramos: If you have TGW it often simplifies management to attach Redwood via TGW - we can request a TGW attachment or peer into a dedicated VPC with non-overlapping space. For large enterprise customers, TGW attachments scale better. Direct VPC peering in cross-region scenarios can be more manual and doesn't scale as well across many accounts.
00:03:56 Tom Wu: How do you handle route table propagation for KV cache/long-lived TCP sessions?
00:04:02 Diego Ramos: We recommend explicit route propagation and tag-based route table rules for the cache subnets. Also set TCP keepalive and connection draining for rolling updates. Sometimes the transcriber puts KV cash but it's KV cache — sorry.
00:04:14 Rajan Patel: KMS questions: do you bring your own key or do you let Redwood encrypt with your key?
00:04:18 Diego Ramos: You can bring your own KMS key. For cloud KMS we do envelope encryption with a customer-managed CMK via cross-account grants. For HSMs we can use an on-prem HSM or a customer HSM in cloud and configure key wrapping. We have a security doc that details the flows — we'll share.
00:04:33 Maya Chen: (interruption) I'll drop the SOC2 and HSM notes after the call.
00:04:36 Lena Park: Great. Another thing — egress controls: we need to ensure logs and telemetry don't leak user content to public telemetry buckets. How does Redwood handle telemetry?
00:04:46 Diego Ramos: We partition telemetry by customer and can disable PII collection. We can also route telemetry to your S3 bucket or Splunk cluster via VPC endpoints. By default hosted telemetry hits our analytics, but for Private we can turn on local telemetry forwarding.
00:04:59 Tom Wu: For private endpoints — do you use provider-privatelink (PrivLink) or internal ALB? Which is easier with TGW?
00:05:08 Diego Ramos: Both are options. PrivateLink (PrivLink) gives single endpoint per service and is easier for per-account access control, but it requires you to accept endpoint service in the console and potentially manage NLBs. Internal ALB is simpler to debug but needs route tables updated. With TGW, PrivateLink can be used but has additional route considerations; TGW attachments with NLB in a dedicated VPC is a common pattern. We'll share architecture diagrams.
00:05:28 Rajan Patel: Are there audit logs for admin actions inside Redwood console when it's private? We need unredacted admin logs forwarded to our SIEM.
00:05:36 Diego Ramos: Yes, admin actions are logged; for private control plane we can ship full admin logs to your SIEM or S3 bucket. Also we support SAML SSO so actions are mapped to your identities.
00:05:45 Maya Chen: Quick check on throughput — what baseline numbers do you usually see for token throughput on a dedicated per-region pool?
00:05:52 Diego Ramos: It depends on model size; for 7B-ish models on A100-equivalent we've seen steady throughput of X tokens/s per GPU (note: filler placeholder in transcript), we usually provide benchmark spreadsheets. For bandwidth between regions, keep an eye on inter-region egress costs — that's a common surprise.
00:06:13 Lena Park: On timeline, we want to pilot in us-east with a small model in Q3 and eu-west by Q4, assuming security sign-off.
00:06:22 Maya Chen: Sounds doable. We'll produce a pilot runbook.
00:06:26 Tom Wu: One more nit: IP whitelisting for our CI runners — can Redwood provide static egress IPs for callbacks?
00:06:33 Diego Ramos: For private deployment you won't need public egress for inference calls but callbacks to your CI might need egress; we can provide NAT'ed egress ranges or use VPC endpoints and private DNS to avoid public IPs.
00:06:48 (crosstalk)
00:06:52 Maya Chen: Okay let's rapid-fire the list of docs we'll share: peering examples, private endpoint options, SOC2/HSM notes, benchmark spreadsheet, TF snippets. Is everyone okay?
00:07:02 Lena Park: Yes please.
00:07:04 Rajan Patel: Also include an explanation of how key rotation is handled.
00:07:07 Diego Ramos: Will do.

[...transcript continues with technical detail and occasional mis-transcriptions...]

00:22:10 Diego Ramos: (screen share referenced) here's an example route table where we tag the Redwood subnets with redwood:service and propagate to TGW, note the blackhole behavior if you accept overlapping routes, always validate CIDR.
00:33:08 Tom Wu: We use NIST-aligned key rotation windows, 90 days. How do you support that?
00:33:12 Diego Ramos: Our key rotation can be orchestrated by your KMS; we support re-wrapping flows and a short blackout window for rekeying, we'll send the procedure.
00:44:05 Lena Park: Any blockers you foresee on the Redwood side?
00:44:09 Diego Ramos: Main blockers are CIDR overlap, need for private control plane, and HSM cert provisioning. If those are resolved we can onboard within 4-6 weeks for a pilot.
00:48:15 Maya Chen: Recap — Verdant Orbit requires private deployment into VPCs, control plane in-customer preferred, KMS/HSM BYOK, audit log forwarding, TGW attachments preferred but PrivateLink acceptable, pilot timeline Q3 in us-east then eu-west Q4. Next steps: we'll send the docs and schedule a net deep-dive. Action items listed in the meta above.
00:48:44 Rajan Patel: Thanks, please mark security notes high priority.
00:48:49 Maya Chen: Absolutely. Thanks all.
